title: Keep awake (Mark 13:28–37)
hook: learn from the fig tree; no one knows the hour; watch

segments.voice: Yesterday, the days of distress, and your line was my words won't pass away. What steady thing did you hold on to? Day two hundred seventeen. The end of a week, and the end of the road to Jerusalem.

Bare sticks on Monday, a green haze by Friday. Nobody needs a calendar to read a tree in spring. Jesus uses exactly that picture, and it's a fig tree again. In the King James Bible: "Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When her branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is near." A few days ago a fig tree in leaf meant disappointment. Now tender leaves are a sign of something coming. After a whole chapter of strange and frightening images, he ends with a tree, and a doorkeeper, and one word.
screen: `A TREE GOES GREEN OVERNIGHT.` → `LEARN A PARABLE OF THE FIG TREE.` → `ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: Then a sentence that stops readers short: "But of that day and that hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father." Not even the Son. Whatever else it means, it leaves no room for anyone to set a date. So what do you do if you can't know when? He tells a tiny story. A man goes on a journey, gives each servant their own work, and tells the doorkeeper to watch. You don't know when the master comes, evening, midnight, cockcrow, or morning: four watches of the night. And some readers notice that Mark's next chapters pass through each of them. An evening supper. A garden at night where friends fall asleep. A rooster crowing. A morning trial. Then the final word of the speech: "And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch." In Greek, grēgoreite, keep awake, stay alert. Watching isn't staring at the sky. The servants in the story are busy with their own work. It's doing today's work awake. Now look back. This week: Caesar's coin, whose wife, the greatest commandment, a widow's mite, not one stone, the days of distress, and keep awake. And the whole road: back on day two hundred it turned south with a question about marriage. Children in his arms. A rich man walking away. Bartimaeus, a borrowed colt, the temple, a rejected stone. Now the road has reached Jerusalem. Tomorrow, the last days begin.
screen: `NOT EVEN THE SON KNOWS THE HOUR.` · `EVENING, MIDNIGHT, COCKCROW, MORNING.` · `GREGOREITE: KEEP AWAKE.` · `THE ROAD HAS REACHED JERUSALEM.` · then, large: `WHAT I SAY UNTO YOU I SAY UNTO ALL, WATCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay awake to today. Settle, and breathe, with your eyes open if you like. Notice five things around you that you've stopped seeing: the light on the wall, the sound of the fridge, the weight of your body in the chair. Then notice what today's work actually is. Not next month's. Today's. The doorkeeper doesn't guard the whole future; just the door, tonight. If you pray, you can ask to be awake to what God is doing right now. The bell holds the time.
Keep awake. No one knows the hour, not even the Son, so the servants do today's work, watchful.
Your line: watch. Today, three times, stop what you're doing, look up, and notice what's actually in front of you. Day two hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Some churches read this passage on the first Sunday of Advent, the season of watchful waiting before Christmas, and some Christians keep vigils or pray at fixed hours as a way of keeping awake.

fork.setup: you're the doorkeeper. the master has left, and you don't know if he's coming at evening, midnight, cockcrow or morning. what do you do?
options: sleep now and wake at dawn.
fork.reveal: watch. "And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch." and some readers find those same four watches in Mark's next chapters.

original.note: Greek: keep awake, watch. the last word of the speech, Mark 13:37.

trapdoor: what you thought: be ready for the end of the world.
what it means: no one knows the hour, so do today's work awake, like a doorkeeper on watch.
what a scholar hears: four night watches named in 13:35, which some readers trace through Mark's passion: supper, Gethsemane, cockcrow, morning.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Hook rewritten: it opened with the banned "Think of". Cut superlatives ("the shortest carry you'll ever get", "the most surprising sentence in the chapter") and the stock "Christians have thought hard about that line for centuries". "Roman" watches and "Mark walks through exactly those four" softened to what some readers notice; "a midnight garden" fixed (Mark gives no hour). Gregory etymology removed from teach, myth and original note under the claims rule. Quotation "to every man his work" in a myth reveal is KJV Mark 13:34.
13:30 ('this generation shall not pass') is not discussed, to keep one idea; Keeper may want a line.

The link between the four watches (13:35) and the passion night (14:17 evening, Gethsemane, 14:72 cockcrow, 15:1 morning) is a widely noted literary observation; 'midnight' for Gethsemane is approximate. Confirm.
